meta.name: Briard First Year Costs
meta.excerpt: The Briard is a large, long-coated herding breed with significant grooming, food, and veterinary costs. This guide breaks down the full first-year budget for new Briard owners.
meta.meta_description: Briard first year costs: puppy price, grooming expenses, food, vet bills, and long-term ownership cost estimates for this ancient French herding breed.

hero.alt: Adult Briard relaxing at home in a family setting

intro.label: Upfront Costs
intro.heading: Bringing Home a Briard: What the First Purchases Actually Cost
intro.html:
A Briard puppy arrives already built for a working life — deep-chested, big-boned, and wrapped in a long, coarse, slightly wavy coat that will eventually reach 6 to 8 inches in length. That combination of size (55–100 lbs at maturity) and coat volume shapes almost every line item below. You're not just buying a large-breed crate; you're buying a grooming toolkit sturdy enough to work through a double coat that mats if neglected for even two or three weeks.

The Acquisition Decision

A puppy from a health-tested breeder who screens for hip dysplasia and eye disease (CSNB/PRA are documented in the breed) runs $1,500–$2,500. Rescue adoption, through a breed-specific network or a regional herding-breed rescue, runs $200–$500 and often includes an adult dog already past the destructive puppy months — a real consideration given how much house a Briard eventually occupies. Because the breed is relatively uncommon in the U.S., expect a waitlist of several months to a year for a reputable breeder litter; budget the adoption fee earlier if timing matters more to you than bloodline.

Gear Sized for a Big, Shaggy Dog

Skip the standard 36-inch crate — a Briard puppy will outgrow it within months. A large or extra-large wire crate with a divider panel ($80–$150) lets the crate grow with the dog instead of being replaced twice. Stainless bowls ($30–$60), a supportive orthopedic-leaning bed ($60–$120) given the breed's joint sensitivity, and a sturdy collar, ID tag, and leash set ($40–$80) round out the basics. Add a long training line ($20–$40) since early leash work and recall practice benefit enormously from this breed's herding brain — Briards think in terms of managing space, and a line lets you safely let that instinct play out during training.

The Grooming Kit Is Non-Negotiable

This is where Briard costs diverge sharply from short-coated breeds. A pin brush, wide-tooth comb, a mat splitter or dematting rake, and a quality detangling spray together run $90–$170 — and this is a purchase you should make before the puppy comes home, not after the first mat appears behind an ear. Baby gates or an exercise pen ($50–$120) help manage a large, curious puppy in the house, and $50–$100 in size-appropriate toys and chews gives that big brain something to do besides your furniture.

Round out the shopping list with the puppy's first veterinary visit ($80–$160), which typically includes an exam, a fecal check, and the start of core vaccinations.

care.label: First Year Recurring
care.heading: Feeding, Grooming, and Vet Costs Through Year One
care.html:
Once the shopping is done, the recurring costs start immediately and don't let up. For a Briard, three categories dominate: veterinary preventive care, food (because this is a large, active dog), and grooming (because of that coat).

Months 1–3: Vaccines and the Setup Tail

The first quarter is when a puppy's medical bills concentrate. The core vaccination series ($200–$400 across several visits) runs alongside deworming and the start of monthly parasite prevention ($200–$400/year). Most vets recommend spay or neuter between 12 and 18 months for large breeds like the Briard, to allow growth plates to close properly given the breed's joint sensitivity — so that $300–$700 expense often lands closer to month 12–18 rather than month one. Puppy kibble formulated for large-breed growth is worth the slightly higher price during this window; it's calibrated to slow calcium uptake and protect developing hips.

Months 4–6: Training and the First Real Coat Maintenance

This is when serious training should start in earnest. Briards are smart and independent — bred to make their own herding decisions rather than wait for constant commands — which makes them wonderful problem-solvers and occasionally stubborn students. A structured puppy class or basic obedience course ($200–$600 across a few sessions) pays off enormously here, channeling that intelligence before it turns into creative destruction of your house. This is also roughly when the coat starts transitioning from puppy fluff to the adult double coat, and twice-weekly line brushing at home becomes essential to prevent early matting.

Months 7–12: Food, Grooming Visits, and Steady State

By month seven, a Briard puppy is eating close to adult portions — a 55–100 lb dog at maturity typically needs 3.5 to 5 cups of quality kibble daily, which is why annual food costs for the breed land at $900–$1,400. Buying a 30-pound bag rather than repeatedly restocking smaller bags is meaningfully more economical per pound and matches how quickly a dog this size goes through food.

Professional grooming typically starts around this stage, once the adult coat is established. Most Briard owners book 5–6 visits per year at $90–$160 per visit ($450–$960/year), because the coat's texture resists simple at-home upkeep once it reaches full length. Add $150–$250 in treats, $120–$250 in enrichment toys (this is a working breed that gets bored and destructive without a job), and $400–$800 if you'll need boarding or pet-sitting during the year.

Insurance Timing

Enroll in pet insurance as early as possible — ideally before any symptoms of hip dysplasia or eye issues appear, since pre-existing conditions are excluded from coverage once diagnosed. At $50–$85/month ($600–$1,020/year), insurance purchased at 8 weeks old locks in coverage for the conditions this breed is statistically more prone to developing later.

special.label: Total & Ongoing
special.heading: First-Year Total, Long-Term Costs, and the Briard's Health Cost Profile
special.html:
Total First Year Estimate: $3,800–$6,500. After year one, ongoing annual costs settle to roughly $2,200–$3,800 — still on the higher end for a dog this size, driven almost entirely by the coat and by insurance premiums that account for the breed's known health tendencies.

What This Breed's Known Health Issues Cost

The Briard's deep chest puts it at real risk for GDV (bloat), a life-threatening emergency requiring surgery within hours of onset. That surgery runs $3,000–$7,000+, and it's one of the strongest arguments for insurance in this breed specifically — GDV strikes suddenly, with no warning symptoms in the weeks prior, and a delayed decision over cost can be fatal. Many owners discuss prophylactic gastropexy with their vet at the time of spay/neuter; the procedure adds to the surgical cost but essentially removes bloat as a future emergency risk.

Hip dysplasia is the other major structural concern in a breed this size and weight. Screening (OFA or PennHIP evaluation) typically costs $200–$450 and is worth requesting from any breeder before purchase. If dysplasia develops and surgery is needed, expect $3,500–$7,000+ per hip. The Briard also carries known eye conditions — Congenital Stationary Night Blindness (CSNB) and progressive retinal atrophy — that warrant periodic ophthalmologist visits at $200–$400 each, especially if a breeder's health testing didn't include a CERF/CAER eye exam on the parents. Cancer, as in most large breeds, remains the biggest wildcard cost, with treatment ranging $2,000–$15,000+ depending on type and stage.

Insurance Choices Shaped by These Risks

Given GDV, hip dysplasia, and hereditary eye disease all appearing in the breed's health profile, a Briard owner should read a policy's orthopedic and hereditary-condition waiting periods closely before enrolling, and ideally lock in coverage while the puppy is young and has no diagnosed conditions yet. A wellness add-on that covers routine exams and vaccines is a reasonable complement to a comprehensive accident-and-illness policy, but the accident-and-illness coverage is the piece that actually protects you from a $5,000 bloat surgery bill.

Budget Path vs. Premium Path: Two Realistic Year-One Totals

Budget path (~$3,900): rescue adoption ($350), basic gear bought on sale ($350), home grooming with a quality tool kit rather than professional visits ($120), no-frills wellness exam and preventives ($500), mid-range large-breed kibble ($950), a single six-week group class ($150), and a modest wellness plan instead of full insurance ($700). This path assumes no major health event and diligent home coat care.

Premium path (~$6,900): breeder puppy with full health testing ($2,200), complete new gear including an orthopedic bed ($550), full vaccination series plus early spay/neuter ($900), premium large-breed food ($1,300), professional grooming every 6–8 weeks ($900), a private trainer alongside group class ($550), and comprehensive insurance enrolled at 8 weeks ($1,000+ premium tier). The gap between paths is almost entirely acquisition method, grooming approach, and insurance tier — not corner-cutting on core welfare.

Home Grooming vs. Professional: The Biggest Lever You Control

Learning to bathe, dry, line-brush, and trim a Briard at home is the single largest cost lever available to an owner, because professional grooming ($450–$960/year) is the one recurring line item that isn't fixed by the dog's biology the way food or vet care is. A quality tool investment ($80–$150 annually in supplies once the initial kit is bought) plus a high-velocity dryer can cut professional visits down to occasional trims, saving $300–$800 per year over the dog's life — but this only works if you commit to twice-weekly brushing sessions; skip a few weeks and the coat mats to the skin, and you'll be back at the groomer paying a dematting surcharge.

Regional Cost Variation

Urban markets on the coasts run 20–40% above the ranges listed here for grooming, boarding, and vet visits — a $90 grooming session in a mid-sized Midwestern city can be $140–$160 in a major coastal metro. Rural and suburban areas generally track closer to the low end of every range, though access to a veterinary ophthalmologist or orthopedic specialist may require travel, adding indirect cost.

Rescue Route: A Real Alternative

Because Briards are a relatively low-volume breed, breed-specific rescues and herding-group rescues periodically place adults and occasionally puppies for $200–$500 — often already spayed/neutered, vaccinated, and temperament-assessed. This route can shave $1,000–$2,000 off the acquisition line versus a breeder puppy, though it comes with less certainty about the dog's genetic health background.

Money-Saving Tactics That Don't Cut Corners

  • Invest in the grooming kit early and use it consistently rather than paying dematting fees later — prevention is always cheaper than the cure with this coat.
  • Buy large-breed puppy food in bulk bags and store it properly; a big dog eating 3.5–5 cups daily burns through smaller bags fast enough that bulk buying is a genuine savings, not just a convenience.
  • Enroll in insurance before any symptoms appear — waiting until after a limp or eye issue shows up means that condition is excluded forever.
  • Choose a group obedience class over one-on-one training for foundational skills, saving private sessions for specific behavioral problems that a class format genuinely can't address.

False economies to avoid: skipping hip and eye screening on a puppy to save money up front, and delaying professional attention to early matting — both tend to cost far more down the line than the initial spend would have.

Lifetime Cost Estimate (10–12 years): $28,000–$52,000+, depending heavily on health outcomes, insurance decisions, and whether grooming is handled at home or professionally.

Quick Answers

Is pet insurance worth it for a Briard?

Given the breed's documented risk for bloat, hip dysplasia, and hereditary eye disease, insurance purchased young is one of the better financial decisions a Briard owner can make. It won't cover pre-existing conditions, so timing the enrollment before any diagnosis matters more for this breed than for many others.

Where do most Briard owners overspend or underspend?

Overspend: buying a full round of adult-size gear before the dog is grown, when a divided crate and adjustable collar would have covered the growth period. Underspend: budgeting for hip and eye screening, which many first-time owners skip entirely and later regret when a health issue could have been caught early.

faq.q: What's the single biggest ongoing expense for a Briard owner?
faq.a: Coat maintenance edges out food as the largest recurring cost beyond the basics. Professional grooming 5–6 times a year at $90–$160 per visit totals $450–$960 annually, and skipping sessions leads to matting that costs even more to correct. Owners who commit to twice-weekly home brushing and occasional professional trims can cut this cost substantially, but the coat never becomes a zero-maintenance line item for this breed.

faq.q: Should I insure my Briard against bloat and hip dysplasia specifically?
faq.a: Yes. Both conditions are well-documented in the breed, and both carry five-figure worst-case price tags — GDV surgery runs $3,000–$7,000+, hip surgery $3,500–$7,000+ per hip. Enroll before any symptoms appear, since pre-existing conditions are permanently excluded once diagnosed. Ask your vet about prophylactic gastropexy at the time of spay/neuter to substantially lower future bloat risk.

faq.q: Can I meaningfully lower costs by grooming my Briard myself?
faq.a: Yes, and it's the most effective lever a Briard owner has. A one-time tool investment of roughly $150–$300 (pin brush, comb, mat splitter, dryer) plus committed twice-weekly line brushing can shrink professional visits to occasional trims, saving $300–$800 a year. This only works with consistency — an inconsistent home routine often ends up costing more once a groomer has to dematt a neglected coat.

faq.q: How does the Briard's exercise and training needs affect first-year budget?
faq.a: Briards need 60–90 minutes of vigorous daily activity and thrive on positive, engaging training rather than rigid drilling — a legacy of their independent herding heritage. This mostly shows up as a time cost rather than a dollar cost, but a structured obedience class ($200–$600) is worth the money for this breed, since a bored, undertrained Briard with pent-up energy is far more likely to become destructive, generating replacement-item costs down the line.

faq.q: Is adopting an adult Briard a realistic way to reduce first-year costs?
faq.a: Yes. Breed-specific and herding-group rescues occasionally place Briards for $200–$500, often already spayed/neutered, vaccinated, and past the destructive puppy stage — shaving $1,000–$2,000 off the acquisition cost compared to a breeder puppy. The trade-off is less certainty about hip and eye health history, so ask the rescue for whatever veterinary records are available before committing.
